title: "The Locked Cabinet"
---

::: {.quest-dialog}
**Prerequisites:** Grow the Carapace. **Objective:** keep keys, settings and sensitive data out of the agent's reach, and know what changes on a shared cluster.
**Time:** about 15 minutes. <span class="ao-badge">General practice (the habits). Mistral facts: Last verified (docs, not run), read 2026-11-20 through a summarising tool (research/mistral.md). Transcript facts: Last verified (docs, not run), read 2026-11-23 (research/transcripts-and-secrets.md). Your own data agreement and cluster policy override anything here.</span>
:::

Much research data is not sensitive. Some of it is, and then special agreements apply. This quest uses no real data and practises **habits**, so that the careful choice becomes automatic.

## Three ideas

1. **A prompt may leave your machine.** With a hosted model, anything the agent reads may be sent to the provider. A model running locally (the Pet, via Ollama) keeps prompts on your machine, though web or tool calls it makes may not. Whether either is allowed for your data is decided by your agreement.
2. **Secrets stay out of content.** API keys, tokens, SSH keys and passwords belong in a secret store, kept out of the project folder, and out of chats and any instructions file you commit. Be aware that an environment variable is visible to any command the agent runs, so a read rule alone is not a seal.
3. **A shared cluster is shared.** What is fine on your laptop can disturb other people on a login node, or break a data policy on shared storage. Cluster rules apply to agents exactly as they apply to you.

::: {.callout-note}
A deny rule on your secrets files (see *Grow the Carapace*) stops the agent's file-reading tool. An agent that can run shell commands may still be able to read them another way, so also keep secrets out of the project folder, and use a sandbox or shell rules where you can. Not confirmed here: exactly how each tool treats shell reads of denied files.
:::

### What the European draft best practices add

The AI for Science best practices (a draft with no endorsements yet; practice 11) say the same about sending data and add three points. Not checked first-hand: read 2026-11-20 through a fetch summary, so re-check the wording on the page; see `research/aiforscience.md`.

- **Reading a file already discloses it.** With an externally hosted model, everything the agent reads goes to the provider. Their example is an agent that opens a project `.env` file: the keys now sit in the provider's logs under your account's retention terms, so rotate them, and keep secrets outside folders the agent can read.
- **Personal data needs more than a no-training promise.** Sending personal data to a provider is processing under GDPR (the EU data protection law). That needs a lawful basis (a legal reason to process), a processor contract (a written agreement with the provider) and, outside the EU, a transfer basis (a legal route for sending data abroad), even when the provider does not train on it. Ask your data steward which accounts are approved (General practice), and use an institutional account for work.
- **Limit where the agent can send data through its environment.** Instructions alone do not stop a send. A sandbox or network limit can.

## What stays behind: transcripts

The agent keeps a record of the session so that it can resume. Anything that passes through a tool goes into that record: file contents, command output, pasted text. Claude Code's docs say that if a tool reads a `.env` file or a command prints a credential, the value is written to the session transcript, stored locally in plaintext (for 30 days by default). Read 2026-11-23 on the docs pages listed in `research/transcripts-and-secrets.md`; no command was run.

A real case: in November 2026 a coding-tool vendor published an account of an incident in which a bucket of agent traces, shared with a vendor for training, was copied. It said a small number of traces held credentials that had not been redacted. We read the vendor's own post; the numbers are theirs.

Habits that cost little:

1. **Reference a secret, do not type it.** Write `psql "$DATABASE_URL"`, so the command, and any rule saved from it, holds a variable's name. When you choose "Yes, and don't ask again", Claude Code saves a rule in `.claude/settings.local.json`, which it keeps out of git through your global excludes only. Reported by users, not confirmed in the docs: a password typed into an approved command can end up in that file.
2. **Approve patterns, not literal commands** (`npm run *`).
3. **Rotate anything that has been in a transcript.** Deleting the file does not reach backups, copies or a vendor's storage.
4. **Keep less.** `cleanupPeriodDays` shortens how long transcripts stay, `claude purge` deletes a project's state (try `--dry-run` first), and `CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_PROMPT_HISTORY=1` skips writing them.
5. **Make a leak worth little (General practice).** A token for one repository that expires in an hour is a small loss if it leaks. GitHub says an installation access token expires after 1 hour. Where a service only issues long-lived keys, give the agent a separate, narrow key that you can rotate without breaking your own work.

Redaction helps and has limits. A scanner matches formats, and a password after `-p` has none. The docs also say deny rules on files do not stop a script the agent runs from reading them.

## Unpublished ideas and results

A common worry: *my unpublished results or ideas will leak and someone will get there first.* Another version is a company showing a proof of something you spent years on. This page does not claim either has happened. The habits below lower the chance and the cost of being wrong.

What the docs say (Claude Code data usage page, read 2026-11-17):

- **Training use** means a provider may learn from your prompts to improve future models. For Free, Pro, Max and Ultra accounts it depends on a privacy setting that you can change. For Team, Enterprise and API accounts, Anthropic says it does not train on code or prompts sent to Claude Code under commercial terms, unless the customer opts in.
- **Retention** for consumer accounts is 5 years if you allow model improvement and 30 days if you do not. Commercial accounts have 30 days as standard, and zero data retention for qualified Enterprise accounts.
- Not checked: the claude.ai chat privacy pages and the full terms. Read the terms of the exact tool and plan you use.

For comparison, Mistral's help and docs pages (read 2026-11-20 through a summarising tool, so re-check the wording before you rely on it; sources in `research/mistral.md`):

- **Training use** depends on the product and plan. Mistral's help pages say that Vibe users are not opted out by default (Vibe Free, Pro, Teams and Student have training on with an opt-out; Vibe Enterprise is opted out by default), and that Mistral Studio's free mode may use data for training. For Studio and the API, the opt-out is in the Admin Panel under Privacy, and opting out of one product does not opt you out of another. For Labs and Public Preview models, the opt-out does not apply.
- **Retention:** we did not find a default retention period on Mistral's own pages. Zero data retention exists for some API requests on pay-as-you-go and each request is reviewed. The page lists Agents, Conversations, Files, Chat and Vibe as excluded (we could not tell whether "Chat" means Le Chat or chat requests). The same page says you do not need zero retention to opt out of model training, so retention and training are separate settings.
- **Location:** the global API endpoint does not commit to an inference location. The EU endpoint (`api.eu.mistral.ai`) is documented as running in EU and EFTA data centers, so a European location needs that endpoint chosen on purpose. We did not confirm where Le Chat or Vibe run.
- Not checked: Le Chat's own privacy page (only a search summary was seen), Mistral's privacy policy, and any other vendor's tools.

The open-weight Mistral models (for example `ministral-3:8b`, Apache 2.0 per Ollama's page) can run locally through Ollama, where the same local-model caveat applies as for any other: prompts stay on your machine, and tool or web calls may still send data out.

Habits:

1. **Keep unpublished ideas, results and sequences out of consumer chat tools** unless the terms say how your text is used and you accept that.
2. **Prefer an agreement your institution has reviewed.** Ask your data steward or research office what is approved. They can give advice on contracts and ownership. This quest gives none.
3. **Consider a local model.** Ollama says it does not see your prompts or data when you run locally (see [Adopt the Pet](../kennel/adopt-the-pet.html)). Tools and web calls the model makes may still send data out. A free hosted tier is not local: see [Free Is Not Free](../kennel/free-is-not-free.html).
4. **Date-stamp your work.** A preprint, a repository tag or a dated lab notebook entry records when you had it.
5. **Share on a need-to-know basis.** Send collaborators what they need for the task.

## Honour-system side quest

Nobody checks this and nothing depends on it. It is here because the real rules are in a document your group holds, and this site cannot see it.

<div data-ao-honour="find-agreement" data-xp="20">Find the data-handling agreement or policy that applies to your project (or ask your group leader where it is). Read the passages about <strong>where data may be processed</strong> and <strong>whether it may be sent to external services</strong>, and write down in your own notes what they say.</div>

<div data-ao-honour="find-secrets" data-xp="10">List where your own API keys and settings files live (for example a <code>.env</code> file or a shell profile), and check that your agent's permission rules deny reading them.</div>

## Lore

*Further reading. Optional.*

- [Data usage](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/data-usage): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it says what is sent to the provider, how training and retention differ by plan, and what telemetry can be turned off. It does not replace your own data agreement.
- [Security](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/security): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it covers prompt injection, credential storage and advice for sensitive code.
- [AI for Science, practice 11: decide where research data may go](https://aiforscience.eu/best-practices/11-decide-where-research-data-may-go/): AI for Science (European draft best practices), docs. Why read: it ties the choice of service to the contract and legal basis for your data, and limits agent sends through the environment. A draft with no endorsements yet; it is not legal advice.
- [Configure permissions](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it shows the deny rules that keep the agent's file tools away from files such as `.env`.
- [The .claude directory](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-directory): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it says what is written to transcripts on disk, how long it stays, and how `claude purge` clears it.
- [Settings](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it explains where "don't ask again" approvals are saved and how `settings.local.json` is kept out of git.
- [An update on our recent security incident](https://cursor.com/blog/security-incident-update): Cursor, article. Why read: a first-hand account of agent traces with unredacted credentials. Our checked notes are in `research/transcripts-and-secrets.md`.
- [Authenticating as a GitHub App installation](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/authenticating-with-a-github-app/authenticating-as-a-github-app-installation): GitHub, docs. Why read: it shows the one-hour token that keeps a leak small.
:::
